name: MAC Lima
funding: Private museum in Barranco. Sponsors include UTEC, Fundación Telefónica Movistar, Fundación BBVA, Credicorp, Bloomberg and the EU delegation. The Getty Foundation gave $64,000 in 2022 for a works-on-paper show.
watch: Sponsor Bloomberg: more than 260 UK artists asked five London theatres to drop Bloomberg Philanthropies in May 2026. The 2022 Getty Foundation grant was one-off.
why_flagged: Sponsor Bloomberg: more than 260 UK artists asked five London theatres to drop Bloomberg Philanthropies in May 2026. The 2022 Getty Foundation grant was one-off.
records_note: Its Auspicios page shows ten sponsor logos with no date.

overview: Contemporary art museum at Av. Grau in the Barranco district of Lima, with three galleries of 100, 200 and 1,000 square metres in an industrial-style building surrounded by a terrace and park (MAC Lima).

Inaugurated in late January 2013 on land donated by the Municipality of Barranco, on the site of the former Barranco Zoo and its artificial lake. It is run as a private non-profit organisation (English Wikipedia).

It succeeds the Instituto de Arte Contemporáneo (IAC), opened in 1955 in the former premises of the Galería de Lima, which moved to Casa Mujica in 1966 and used the Museum of Italian Art building from 1969 to 1972 (English Wikipedia).
Architect: Frederick Cooper Llosa (English Wikipedia).
The Spanish Wikipedia infobox lists Pedro Pablo Alayza as director and Eduardo Hochschild Beeck as president.

The museum's programme includes the education programmes Escuela Vecina, #aulamac and Domingos en el MAC (Spanish Wikipedia), and Contemporáneo 1, a permanent collection exhibition opened in December 2024 (English Wikipedia).
Open Tuesday to Sunday 10:00 to 19:00, closed Monday (MAC Lima).
details.funding_verdict: MAC Lima: private non-profit, on land from the Barranco municipality
funding: English Wikipedia states that the museum is run as a private non-profit organisation and was built on land donated by the Municipality of Barranco; Spanish Wikipedia describes the site as land ceded in concession by the district municipality.
Spanish Wikipedia states that a 1990s auction brought in geometric art by artists including Jesús Rafael Soto and Carlos Cruz-Diez for the collection.

red_flags.heading: 2018 petition against the exhibition "Canon"
points: "Canon: Vírgenes de la Puerta" by Juan José Barboza-Gubo and Andrew Mroczek opened at MAC Lima on 7 February 2018 and ran through 1 April; a parallel show, "Canon: Los Chicos and Anda", was at the Cultural Center of Spain (The Advocate, Advocate.com Editors, "Trans Photography Under Attack In Peru", 27 February 2018).

A CitizenGo petition was addressed to Luis Tejada Chacón, director of the Spanish Cooperation Agency for International Development, to Enrique Stiglich, director of the Museum of Contemporary Art in Lima, and to Ernesto de Zulueta Habsburgo-Lorraine, Spain's ambassador to Peru. It demanded the closing of the exhibitions and had more than 20,000 signatures by 27 February 2018; the groups the article names are Tradición y Acción por un Perú Mayor, Revuelta Contra el Arte Moderno and the Asociación Antonin Scalia (The Advocate).

Spanish Wikipedia states that conservative groups and congressman Carlos Tubino denounced the exhibition as blasphemous, which led to a bill to criminalise religious defamation, and that the museum publicly defended the works.

details.bottom_line: MAC Lima is a private non-profit museum built on land from the Barranco municipality. The documented issue is the 2018 CitizenGo petition, addressed to the museum's director and to Spain's ambassador, demanding the closing of its "Canon" exhibition.

name: Galeria Foksal (Foksal Gallery)
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Non-profit contemporary art gallery on Foksal Street, Warsaw, housed in an annexe to the Zamoyski Palace (stated by the gallery).

Founded in 1966 by the critics Wiesław Borowski, Anka Ptaszkowska and Mariusz Tchorek and artists including Tadeusz Kantor and Henryk Stażewski. Borowski was nominally its director for nearly 35 years (stated by the gallery).
Named for Foksal Street, where it stands (stated by the gallery). Wikipedia dates the opening to 1 April 1966 with Zbigniew Gostomski's "Optical Objects".
Interior designed by the artists Zbigniew Gostomski, Edward Krasiński and Zygmunt Targowski, including the cabinets, bookshelves and chairs, which remain unchanged (stated by the gallery).
Before it joined its present institution it operated under the Visual Arts Studio until 1984 and then the Warsaw Agency for Art Exhibitions (stated by the gallery).
Current curators named on the contact page: Zuzanna Mielczarek (programme curator), Katarzyna Krysiak and Martyna Stołpiec.
Visiting: free admission. Open Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday noon to 6 PM, Thursday noon to 7 PM, Saturday noon to 4 PM. Online sign language interpreting is offered.
details.funding_verdict: Galeria Foksal: public: the regional government of Mazovia
funding: The gallery is part of the Mazovian Institute of Culture (formerly the Mazovian Centre for Culture and Arts), "financed by the Marshal Office of the Province of Mazovia" (stated by the gallery). The Marshal Office is the Mazovia regional government.
Wikipedia likewise describes the gallery as government funded through the Mazovia Region Centre for Culture and Art.
not_related: the Foksal Gallery Foundation at Górskiego Street, Warsaw. It was established at the gallery in 1997, and some of its members later left to set up a separate institution; the gallery states it is "a separate body, without any direct links with Foksal Gallery". Wikipedia describes the foundation as a commercial entity that left the gallery in 2001.
details.bottom_line: The money behind Galeria Foksal is public: it is part of a regional cultural institute financed by the Mazovia provincial government. The commercial Foksal Gallery Foundation is a separate organisation.

name: Muzeum Sztuki in Łódź (ms1 & ms2)
funding: Public museum funded by the city and the Ministry of Culture.
watch: No ORLEN, PGE or Azoty link found.
records_note: Posts activity reports for 2016 to 2025, profit and loss accounts for 2016 to 2023 and its 15-member museum council.
finances_note: Calendar 2023 income PLN 26.0M: about 94 percent public subsidies (budget subsidy 16.9M plus other grants 7.6M), 4 percent sales of goods; no donations line (profit and loss account).
affiliations_note: Runs the Herbst Palace Museum as a branch, shares the Łódź Voivodeship parent with seven regional institutions, and has worked with MoMA's Post platform since 2013. Member of CIMAM.
highlight: Władysław Strzemiński designed the Neoplastic Room at ms1 in 1948 to house his own and Katarzyna Kobro's spatial sculptures.

overview: Museum of modern and contemporary art in Łódź with two main sites: ms1 in the former palace of the industrialist Maurycy Poznański, which holds Władysław Strzemiński's Neoplastic Room, and ms2 at ul. Ogrodowa 19, a converted 19th century spinning mill of the Izrael Poznański factory (Wikipedia; museum website).

Origins in the avant-garde group "a.r." (Władysław Strzemiński and Katarzyna Kobro were members), whose International Collection of Modern Art opened to the public on 15 February 1931. It moved to the Poznański palace in 1948 (Wikipedia).
ms2 opened in autumn 2008 with about 3,000 square metres for the permanent collection and 600 for temporary exhibitions (Wikipedia).

Director: Daniel Muzyczuk, appointed by the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage after a selection committee recommended him unanimously. He had been acting director since July 2024 (ArtReview, 11 August 2025).

Visiting: ms1 and ms2 exhibitions are open Tuesday and Wednesday 9:00 to 16:00, Thursday 12:00 to 18:00, Friday 12:00 to 20:00, Saturday and Sunday 12:00 to 18:00, closed Monday. The museum joined the "Muzeum za 1 zł" scheme for people aged 8 to 26 (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Muzeum Sztuki: public: a cultural institution of the Łódź Voivodeship self-government, co-financed by the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage
funding: The footer of the museum's website names the Łódź Voivodeship self-government (Samorząd Województwa Łódzkiego) as its organiser and the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage as co-financier. Notes from Poland (Piotr Kosiewski, 26 September 2022) says the museum is administered jointly by the ministry and the marshal of Łódź province.

Wikipedia reports that the regeneration of ms2 was funded by the EU's Integrated Regional Development Operational Programme, the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, the Voivodeship Office and the Marshal Office in Łódź.

red_flags.heading: Director Jarosław Suchan removed in 2022
points: Jarosław Suchan, director since 2006, was told at the end of April 2022, at a meeting with deputy culture minister Jarosław Sellin, that he was dismissed. He said: "I didn't get any explanation." The Art Newspaper (Anny Shaw, 30 May 2022) says Poland's ruling Law and Justice party did not renew his contract in November.

Notes from Poland (Piotr Kosiewski, deputy director of the Batory Foundation's ideaForum, 26 September 2022) writes that the culture ministry would not allow Suchan a further term, that "the marshal's opposition" of Łódź province stood in the way, and that he was dismissed overnight without a specific reason. It says the ministry and the marshal administer the museum jointly.

The Art Newspaper says the Polish government replaced him with the artist Andrzej Biernacki, who has run the private Browarna Gallery in Łowicz since 1991 and has no experience running a public institution, and who plans to shift the collection's focus from international artists to Polish artists, especially from Łódź. Culture minister Piotr Gliński told PAP that the main reason for the nomination was Biernacki's views (Notes from Poland).

Richard Armstrong of the Guggenheim called the removal a "shock to the museum community worldwide" in a letter to Gliński; Glenn Lowry of MoMA and Maria Balshaw of Tate also condemned it, and a Polish contemporary art community open letter criticised Biernacki's appointment (The Art Newspaper).

Kosiewski argues that the ministry's handling of the museum, including Biernacki's appointment without competition, shows ideologically driven personnel choices that undermine competence and public trust (Notes from Poland).
Daniel Muzyczuk, acting director since July 2024, took over from Biernacki (ArtReview).

press.overall: The criticism concerns the 2022 dismissal of the director, not the museum's programme.

items.title: Anny Shaw, with Gareth Harris, "'A shock to the community worldwide': directors of Tate, Guggenheim and MoMA condemn ousting of Polish museum head" (30 May 2022)
points: Reports that Suchan's contract was not renewed by the Law and Justice party and that he was dismissed without explanation, and that the government replaced him with an artist without museum experience.
Armstrong links the case to the departures of the directors of the Zachęta National Gallery and the National Museum in Warsaw and calls it a move to reduce these museums to "ideological puppets".

details.bottom_line: The museum is a public institution of the Łódź Voivodeship, co-financed by the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, with EU and ministry money behind the ms2 building. The documented weak point is the 2022 removal of director Jarosław Suchan, which Notes from Poland attributes to the ministry, and the government's installation of Andrzej Biernacki, followed by Daniel Muzyczuk's takeover as acting director in 2024 and his appointment by the ministry in 2025.

name: Wrocław Contemporary Museum
funding: The pages read did not state its funders or budget. The President of Wrocław appoints its acting director, which indicates municipal control (City of Wrocław, 16 January 2020).
watch: Museum at pl. Strzegomski 2. Its first director Andrzej Jarosz died on 10 December 2019 and Piotr Lisowski became acting director on 16 January 2020 (City of Wrocław, 16 January 2020).
records_note: The site lists a public information bulletin (BIP) link; not opened.

overview: The Wrocław Contemporary Museum is at pl. Strzegomski 2, 53-681 Wrocław (museum website).

Its director Andrzej Jarosz died on 10 December 2019; the President of Wrocław entrusted Piotr Lisowski, a curator there since December 2016, with the acting director's duties from 16 January 2020 (City of Wrocław).
What is there: the site links a virtual museum of objects and a loans page; the pages read give no collection figures.
The pages read describe no archive.
details.funding_verdict: Wrocław Contemporary Museum: funding not stated in the pages read
funding: The pages read did not state the museum's grants, budget or sponsors.
No reporting found of funding or a director row in the pages read.
details.bottom_line: Funding unconfirmed. The city's role in appointing leadership is the one documented link. A 2022 director row named in the lead was not found.

name: Serralves Foundation
records_note: Serralves posts yearly reports with audited accounts from 1989 to 2020 and names founders.
finances_note: FY2024 income EUR 16.9M: about 39 percent public subsidy, 24 percent patronage (2.5M of it under the residence-permit law), 36 percent sales and services (Relatorio e Contas 2024, note 15).
affiliations_note: Primary partner with Mudam, Bozar, CAC Vilnius, TEA Tenerife and Triennale Milano Teatro in the PIT performance-art initiative. The Portuguese State is a founder since 1989.

overview: Contemporary art museum, villa and about 18 hectares of park in Porto, run by the Fundação de Serralves (Wikipedia).

The State bought the estate in 1986. The park opened to the public on 29 May 1987. The Foundation was created in 1989 as a partnership between the State and about 51 public and private bodies (Wikipedia).
The villa, Casa de Serralves, was built between 1925 and 1944 for the second Count of Vizela, to designs by José Marques da Silva (Wikipedia).
The museum was designed by Álvaro Siza Vieira and opened on 6 June 1999: 13,000 m2 with 14 galleries (Wikipedia).
Visiting: general ticket EUR 24. Park only EUR 15. Free for children under 12. Free entry on the first Sunday of each month is listed among the residents' discounts (Serralves website).
details.funding_verdict: Serralves Foundation: mixed: State co-financing plus founders from Portuguese business and municipalities
funding: Founders: Wikipedia counts 181 founders. The Foundation's page of "Patron Founders", Founders who contributed to the Annual Fund, lists names for 2021 to 2024 with no amounts, among them Galp Energia (all four years) and Tabaqueira (2021 and 2022).
State: the page shows the Portuguese Republic under "Co-financing". The Bloco de Esquerda said in October 2024 that state funding was set at EUR 6.4 million that year (Lusa, via Observador).

red_flags.heading: Fossil fuels
points: Galp Energia is a Patron Founder in each year from 2021 to 2024 (Serralves website). Galp's units include oil and gas exploration and production and crude oil refining (Wikipedia).

red_flags.heading: Tobacco
points: Tabaqueira, S.A. is a Patron Founder in 2021 and 2022, and absent from the 2023 and 2024 lists (Serralves website). Wikipedia's page on the Português cigarette brand describes Tabaqueira, its maker, as a subsidiary of Philip Morris International.

red_flags.heading: Protest over the 2018 Mapplethorpe show
points: Artistic director João Ribas resigned on 21 September 2018 (Observador); on 24 September an open letter to Foundation president Ana Pinho, signed by more than 150 artists and arts professionals, condemned the removal of 20 works and the age restriction (The Art Newspaper). Protesters gathered outside (ArtReview).

State bodies: on 24 September 2018 the state inspectorate IGAC told Lusa that art exhibitions need no age classification (CM Jornal). On 25 September Porto mayor Rui Moreira asked for an urgent meeting of its Founders' Council (CM Jornal). On 16 October the parliamentary culture committee heard Ribas and the board, who gave opposing accounts (Observador).

press.overall: Criticism concentrates on the 2018 Mapplethorpe exhibition, when the board and its artistic director disagreed in public.

items.title: Gareth Harris and José da Silva, "Wolfgang Tillmans and Tania Bruguera pledge support for censored Serralves museum director" (2018)
points: Ribas resigned after 20 works were removed from the Mapplethorpe show and two galleries were limited to visitors aged 18 and over.
More than 150 artists and arts professionals signed a letter to Foundation president Ana Pinho; it called the use of Portuguese law on "pornographic" material "disingenuous and insulting".
The Foundation said the 20 works were left out by the curator alone and it was not censorship.

items.title: news desk, "Serralves Museum removes Mapplethorpe works, artistic director resigns" (2018)
points: Reports the removals, the age-restricted rooms and the resignation.
The museum said it receives almost one million visitors a year and that the public should be alerted.

items.title: no author named, "Censorship and controversy at the Serralves Contemporary Art Museum of Porto" (2018)
points: Argues the Foundation's action replicates the US culture wars of the 1980s and 1990s.
Reports that collector Luiz Teixeira de Freitas wrote in solidarity with Ribas and asked for the return of 700 drawings he had lent.
Reports that the Foundation's leaders deny censorship.

items.title: Rita Cipriano and Gonçalo Correia, "João Ribas: demiti-me porque não podia tolerar a censura em Serralves" (2018)
points: Ribas told the parliamentary culture committee on 16 October 2018 that two works were removed an hour before the press conference. Board member José Pacheco Pereira said it was false that two works were removed.

details.bottom_line: The Foundation is funded by the State and by Portuguese business founders, and the Annual Fund list is public by name though not by amount. The weak points are two named patron founders, Galp Energia (2021 to 2024) and Tabaqueira (2021 and 2022), and the September 2018 dispute over the Mapplethorpe show, where the board and Ribas gave opposing accounts. Watch for amounts per founder.

name: Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico
funding: Private nonprofit. Current exhibitions are backed by the Flamboyan Foundation, Helen Frankenthaler Foundation and the Puerto Rico Tourism Company.
watch: On 19 November 2023 activists picketed after the Cecilia Orta Allende gallery was renamed for a donor family tied to the Fiscal Oversight Board.
why_flagged: Private nonprofit. Current exhibitions are backed by the Flamboyan Foundation, Mellon Foundation, Helen Frankenthaler Foundation, Mano Amiga and the Puerto Rico Tourism Company. No corporate donors are named.
records_note: Form 990s for 2000 to 2025 are on ProPublica.
finances_note: FY2025 income USD 7.3M: about 19 percent government grants, 31 percent donations and memberships, 14 percent earned, rest investments, events and admissions (Form 990, Part VIII).
affiliations_note: A Smithsonian Affiliate accredited by the American Alliance of Museums, working with the University of Puerto Rico and the Alliance of Museums of Puerto Rico on Tiznando el País. Member of AAMD.

overview: Art museum at 299 Avenida de Diego in Santurce, San Juan, showing Puerto Rican art from the 18th century to the present (museum site).

Opened on 1 July 2000. The concept dates to 1995, when the Puerto Rico Tourism Company, with funding from the Government Development Bank, chose to incorporate the old hospital rather than demolish it (Wikipedia).

Housed in the former San Juan Municipal Hospital, designed by architect William H. Shimmelphening and completed in 1920. It was a hospital until 1966, then offices of the Department of Transportation and Public Works until 1975. Planners built the new museum around the old structure (Wikipedia).
Permanent collection includes José Campeche's "Virgen de la Soledad de la Victoria" (1782 to 1789) (Wikipedia). The museum also has a sculpture garden (museum site).
Open Wednesday, Friday and Saturday 10:00 to 17:00, Thursday 10:00 to 20:00 with free admission from 17:00 to 20:00, Sunday 11:00 to 17:00. Closed Monday, Tuesday and holidays (museum site).
details.funding_verdict: Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico: private non-profit: contributions and earned income, with filed accounts and no published donor list
funding: Public filings: the museum files as Museo De Arte De Puerto Rico Inc (EIN 66-0537284). Revenue was $7,308,690 in fiscal 2025 and $12,360,346 in fiscal 2024; contributions were 50.2 percent of revenue in 2025 and 76.2 percent in 2024. Net assets were $18,599,436 in 2025 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).

Gloria Benítez and José Carrión III are "aportadores económicos" of the museum, and Benítez is secretary of its Junta de Síndicos (board of trustees), according to journalist Sandra Rodríguez Cotto. Carrión is a former president of the island's Fiscal Oversight Board (Amsterdam News).

red_flags.heading: Protest over the Cecilia Orta Allende gallery
points: Naming: in May 2022 the museum mounted a wooden plaque with the name and likeness of artist-activist Cecilia Orta Allende in a first-floor gallery. By late August 2023 the plaque was gone (Amsterdam News).

Donor family: the Amsterdam News reports that the gallery now bears the name of Valeria Antonia Carrión Benítez, only daughter of donors Gloria Benítez and José Carrión III. The museum says it kept Orta Allende's name on the space, now the Galería-Taller Cecilia Orta Allende, and that galleries are named for sponsors, not artists (Rodríguez Cotto). It says the space grew from 731 to 1,157.5 square feet.

Protest: on 19 November 2023 Afro Puerto Rican activists picketed the museum over the plaque (Amsterdam News). Led by Edwin Velázquez Collazo and others, they called the decision "un acto discriminatorio, racista y elitista" (Rodríguez Cotto, my translation: a discriminatory, racist and elitist act).
Museum response: executive director María Cristina Gaztambide said the plaque was moved to the Center for Educational Innovation, not eliminated (Amsterdam News).
Estate: José Antonio Orta, representing the Orta Allende estate, said attempts to meet the board and director failed (Rodríguez Cotto).

not_related: Museo De Arte Contemporaneo De Puerto Rico Inc (EIN 66-0420190). It files separately from this museum in the ProPublica listing.

press.overall: The dispute was covered by a New York Black newspaper and a Puerto Rican journalist's Substack.

wider_context: Carrión was appointed to the federal board overseeing Puerto Rico's finances in 2016. University of Puerto Rico professor Emilio Pantojas raised a conflict of interest because Carrión is the brother-in-law of Resident Commissioner Pedro Pierluisi, and Senator Bernie Sanders said the board included "architects of the crisis" (Bond Buyer, 2016).
Carrión and Gloria Benítez are named as museum donors, and Benítez is secretary of its board of trustees (Rodríguez Cotto, Amsterdam News).
details.bottom_line: The museum's income is contributions and earned revenue, with filed accounts but no published donor list. The weak point is the 2022 to 2023 plaque removal and gallery renaming tied to a trustee family, which drew a picket in November 2023 and gave two accounts (renamed, or name kept). Worth watching: whether the museum publishes who funds each named gallery.

name: Katara Cultural Village
funding: The page read does not state who funds Katara. It reports a Build-Operate-Transfer partnership with A Triple Company for the Chedi Katara hotel, opened in November 2022.
watch: Doha's cultural village, run by the Cultural Village Foundation (Katara), whose general manager is Dr Khalid bin Ibrahim Al Sulaiti. Qatar Tribune (13 Nov 2022) called its hotel deal the first public-private partnership in hospitality and hotel projects.
records_note: No accounts were found in the pages read.

overview: A destination in Doha that Qatar Tribune describes as combining culture, tourism and entertainment, run by the Cultural Village Foundation, known as Katara (Qatar Tribune, 13 Nov 2022).
The pages read give no founding date and no collection.
What is there: the pages read name the Chedi Katara Hotel and Resort, 59 rooms and suites and 32 villas and chalets, inaugurated on a Saturday in November 2022 (Qatar Tribune, 13 Nov 2022).
Archive: the pages read describe none.
details.funding_verdict: Katara Cultural Village: state-linked foundation; funders not stated in the page read
funding: The Chedi Katara was a partnership between Katara and A Triple Company under a Build-Operate-Transfer arrangement; Sheikh Abdul Rahman bin Abdullah bin Ghanem Al Thani chairs A Triple's board (Qatar Tribune, 13 Nov 2022).
No reporting found, in the pages read, of Katara's grants, budget or its relation to Qatar Foundation.
wider_context: Qatar Tribune (13 Nov 2022) says the hotel's opening coincided with preparations to host the football World Cup; Dr Al Sulaiti said Katara had succeeded in encouraging investment in tourism through cooperation with the private sector.
details.bottom_line: The page read gives only the 2022 hotel partnership and no funding figures. The foundation's income and its link to the state remain to be established from other sources.
details.website: https://www.katara.net (opened 2026-11-18; live, the page text read was only the title)

name: Msheireb Museums
funding: The pages read did not state a budget or funders for Msheireb Museums. The Art Newspaper (26 November 2015) said the $5.5bn Msheireb redevelopment that includes the museums is backed by Sheikha Mozah bint Nasser.
watch: Four historic houses in Downtown Doha turned into museums in October 2015, one of them Bin Jelmood House, which covers the Indian Ocean slave trade and modern exploitation. The Art Newspaper described the complex as Qatar's latest bid to rebrand itself as a culture hub.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: Four museums in restored historic houses in the Msheireb quarter of Downtown Doha (The Art Newspaper, 26 November 2015).
The four museums opened in October 2015 as part of the Msheireb quarter; Hafiz Ali Ali is director of the museums (The National, 23 May 2016).

What is there: the four houses cover Qatar's change after oil was found in 1939, Doha's architecture, family life in 20th-century Qatar, and in Bin Jelmood House the history of the global slave trade (The Art Newspaper, 26 November 2015). Opening displays included a slave sales contract on a clay tablet and Greek paintings of enslaved workers on an olive plantation (The National, 23 May 2016).

Archive: the museum drew on manumission documents from the British political agent in Manama, oral histories from a few Qatari families and archival material on Qataris' part in the trade (The National, 23 May 2016). The pages read did not describe a public archive or library.
details.funding_verdict: Msheireb Museums: the pages read did not state funders; the surrounding redevelopment is backed by Sheikha Mozah bint Nasser.
funding: The Art Newspaper (26 November 2015): the $5.5bn Msheireb redevelopment that includes the museums is backed by Sheikha Mozah bint Nasser, second wife of Qatar's former emir.
No reporting found, in the pages read, of the museums' own budget or grants.

red_flags.heading: Labour conditions of builders
points: The Art Newspaper (26 November 2015) noted that human rights organisations had criticised Qatar over poor conditions for migrant workers who built stadiums and museums ahead of the 2022 World Cup.
Hafiz Ali Ali, museums director, said the museum was not a response to criticism of Qatar's treatment of World Cup construction workers (The National, 23 May 2016).

red_flags.heading: Contested history inside Qatar
points: An unnamed consultant told The National (23 May 2016) that some Qataris, descendants of both slaves and slave owners, objected to the museum and many declined to give oral histories, so the museum does not examine in depth how slavery's legacy shapes Qatari society today.
Kristin Smith Diwan of the Arab Gulf States Institute said the broader focus on exploitation helps Qatar appear open to global challenges (The National, 23 May 2016).

details.bottom_line: The pages read point to the Msheireb redevelopment, backed by Sheikha Mozah bint Nasser, as the money behind the museums; no budget was found. The contested points are labour conditions during Qatar's building programme and the reluctance of Qataris to give oral histories.

name: tranzit.ro
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Romanian non-governmental organisation for contemporary art, "initiated and funded by ERSTE Foundation", announced on 15 December 2011 and fully active from early 2012 with centres in Bucharest, Iași and Cluj (e-flux).
Five people were chosen through a closed call to run it: Matei Bejenaru, Livia Pancu, Lia Perjovschi, Attila Tordai-S and Raluca Voinea (e-flux).

It is the fifth member of the tranzit.org network, which also has members in Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the Slovak Republic. The network was founded in 2002 and ERSTE Foundation has been its main partner since 2010 (e-flux).
The Cluj space is at Sámuel Brassai Street 5, open on weekdays from 15:00 to 18:00 (myartguides). It describes itself as working in three permanent spaces, in Iași, Cluj and Bucharest (myartguides).
funding: ERSTE Foundation initiated tranzit.ro and funds it (e-flux, 15 December 2011). Temporary Art Review (Adriana Ledecouvreur, 6 April 2017) calls ERSTE Foundation the primary financial supporter, with additional applications to Romanian state funds, the Goethe-Institut and EU programmes.

Wikipedia calls ERSTE Foundation the biggest Austrian savings bank foundation and the main anchor shareholder of Erste Group Bank AG, using part of its dividend income to fund projects in Central and South Eastern Europe.

press.overall: One Q&A profile, not a critical review, which describes the funding conditions of the Romanian art scene.

items.title: Adriana Ledecouvreur, "tranzit.ro" (2017)
points: The introduction says financing artistic projects in post-communist economies "demonstrates a particular (old) mixture of arts, culture, financing and politics."
An unnamed respondent says the local art scene is "constantly menaced by underfunding".
Not criticism of the institution: the answers come from the tranzit.ro team.

details.bottom_line: The money behind tranzit.ro is ERSTE Foundation, which started the organisation in 2011 and pays for it from dividends on its Erste Group Bank stake, supplemented, according to Temporary Art Review (2017), by applications to Romanian state funds, the Goethe-Institut and EU programmes.

name: Ruarts Foundation
watch: Foundation founded 2003. It opened its own building in 2021 and runs street-art grants. Sardarov is not on EU, UK or US sanctions lists.
why_flagged: Foundation founded 2003. It opened its own building in 2021 and runs street-art grants. Sardarov is not on EU, UK or US sanctions lists.
records_note: Its About page names founder Marianna Sardarova and art director Catherine Borissoff.
affiliations_note: Founded by collector Marianna Sardarova, who also set up the separate RuArts Gallery; it states it works with state museums but names no standing partner.

overview: Private contemporary art foundation and exhibition space at Trubnikovsky Lane 6, Moscow. Its stated mission is to "study, systematise, examine and promote Russian art".
Founded in 2003 by collector Marianna Sardarova, who told The Blueprint the idea came to her in 2003. Art director is Catherine Borissoff (spelled Katrin Borisov in Russian press).
The foundation's six-storey building opened on 17 April 2021 with the exhibition "Soft Homeland" (Moskvich Mag, The Blueprint; names of the architect and floor area not given in either).
The building holds exhibition halls, a library, an educational centre, a bookshop and a café (The Blueprint, 2021).
Collection of more than 2,000 works, focused on unofficial Soviet art and contemporary Russian art. Sections of the site cover Now, Archive, Publishing, Auction and Grants (stated by the foundation).

Its older gallery on Ostozhenka is closing after 21 years. The last show runs from 18 September to 4 October 2026, and the foundation continues at Trubnikovsky Lane with a programme booked to 2028 (Moskvich Mag, 10 September 2026).
Visiting: open Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 to 20:00. Admission was paid at the 2021 opening, and no current price was found.
details.funding_verdict: Ruarts Foundation: private foundation: no funder, accounts or donor list published
funding: The foundation's About page says it was established in 2003 by collector and philanthropist Marianna Sardarova (stated by the foundation).

Transparency International Russia, an anti-corruption group, wrote on 21 March 2025 that Rashid Sardarov, owner of the oil and gas company JSC South Ural Industrial Company, and his wife Marianna are citizens of St Kitts and Nevis, citing a February 2024 French company registry document. The Ruarts founder has the same name.
details.bottom_line: Ruarts is a private foundation whose money is not disclosed. It publishes no accounts, board or donor list. The only point is that the founder's name matches the name Transparency International Russia gives for the wife of Rashid Sardarov, an oil and gas owner; no source opened ties his money to the foundation. Watch for any published funding statement.
